Every running command has a list of the files it has open, the File Descriptor Table. The index in this table is the file descriptor, and the first three are always there: File descriptor Name The command uses it to Redirect By default, in a terminal 0 stdin, the standard input read its input < comes from the keyboard 1 stdout, the standard output write its results > goes to the display 2 stderr, the standard error write its error messages 2> goes to the display A command reads its input from 0, writes its results to 1 and its error messages to 2. It does not know what is behind them. Before it starts the command, the shell can connect any of them to a file: this is a redirect.

Redirect What it does command > file Writes the output (1) into file. The file is emptied first, or created command >> file Appends the output to the end of file command 2> file Writes the errors (2) into file command 2>> file Appends the errors to the end of file command > out 2> err The output into out, the errors into err command &> file Both the output and the errors into file command > file 2>&1 The same, written in the older way: "2 goes where 1 goes" command < file Reads the input (0) from file, instead of the keyboard danger > empties the file before the command starts, even if the command fails. ls > notes.txt deletes everything that was in notes.txt. Use >> when you want to keep the old content.

[student@fedora lab03]$ ls Music > list.txt [student@fedora lab03]$ cat list.txt jazz.mp3 pop.mp3 rock.mp3 [student@fedora lab03]$ echo "--- end ---" >> list.txt [student@fedora lab03]$ cat list.txt jazz.mp3 pop.mp3 rock.mp3 --- end --- [student@fedora lab03]$ echo "new" > list.txt [student@fedora lab03]$ cat list.txt new ls Music > list.txt printed nothing on the display: its output went into list.txt, which was created. >> added a line at the end of the file. The last > emptied the file and wrote only new.

Error messages are written to 2, not to 1. A > alone does not redirect them: [student@fedora lab03]$ ls Music /nope > list.txt ls: cannot access '/nope': No such file or directory [student@fedora lab03]$ ls Music /nope > list.txt 2> errors.txt [student@fedora lab03]$ cat errors.txt ls: cannot access '/nope': No such file or directory [student@fedora lab03]$ ls /nada 2>> errors.txt [student@fedora lab03]$ cat errors.txt ls: cannot access '/nope': No such file or directory ls: cannot access '/nada': No such file or directory [student@fedora lab03]$ ls Music /nope &> all.txt [student@fedora lab03]$ cat all.txt ls: cannot access '/nope': No such file or directory Music: jazz.mp3 pop.mp3 rock.mp3 With > list.txt, the list went into the file, but the error still appeared on the display. With 2> errors.txt, the error went into its own file, and 2>> added a second error at the end of it. With &>, both the list and the error went into the same file.

< gives a command a file instead of the keyboard. The command reads its input from 0 and does not know that it is a file: [student@fedora lab03]$ sort < fruits.txt apple apple apple banana banana cherry kiwi [student@fedora lab03]$ wc -l fruits.txt 7 fruits.txt [student@fedora lab03]$ wc -l < fruits.txt 7 sort read the lines from fruits.txt and printed them in alphabetical order. wc -l fruits.txt counted the lines of a file that it opened by itself, so it knows its name and prints it. With <, the shell opened the file and gave it to wc as its input: wc does not know any name, so it prints only the number. tip Run sort without anything: it reads from the keyboard. Type a few words, one per line, then press Ctrl+D (end of input): sort prints them in order. In the same way, cat > notes.txt saves everything you type into notes.txt, until you press Ctrl+D.

A pipe connects the output (1) of a command to the input (0) of the next one, without any file in between: [student@fedora lab03]$ ls /usr/bin | wc -l 1843 [student@fedora lab03]$ ls -l /usr/bin | less ls /usr/bin | wc -l counted the programs in /usr/bin: ls wrote the names, one per line, and wc -l counted the lines. ls -l /usr/bin | less showed the long list one screen at a time, instead of letting it run off the screen. Command What it does with its input sort Sorts the lines in alphabetical order uniq Removes the lines that repeat the line right above them wc -l Counts the lines head -n <N> Keeps the first N lines head -c <N> Keeps the first N bytes tail -n <N> Keeps the last N lines grep <text> Keeps the lines that contain text less Shows it one screen at a time, like man (quit with q) Searching for a text: grep​ grep prints only the lines that contain a text. It reads the files given as parameters, or its input when there are none, so it works at the end of a pipe too: [student@fedora lab03]$ grep apple fruits.txt apple apple apple [student@fedora lab03]$ grep -c apple fruits.txt 3 [student@fedora lab03]$ grep -i APPLE fruits.txt apple apple apple [student@fedora lab03]$ grep student /etc/group wheel:x:10:student student:x:1000: [student@fedora lab03]$ ps | grep bash 2817 pts/0 00:00:00 bash grep apple fruits.txt printed the three lines of fruits.txt that contain apple; -c only counted them. -i ignores the difference between upper and lower case letters. grep student /etc/group showed the groups of student: its own group, and wheel, the group of the users that are allowed to use sudo. ps | grep bash kept only the line of bash from the list of ps. Option What it does -i Ignores upper and lower case -c Prints only how many lines contain the text -v Prints the lines that do not contain the text -n Prints the line number in front of every line it finds -r Searches in all the files of a directory, and of its subdirectories tip Put the text between quotes when it has spaces: grep 'model name' /proc/cpuinfo. Repeated Lines: uniq​ uniq removes a line when it is the same as the line right above it. It compares only neighbor lines, so it is almost always used after sort, which puts the same lines next to each other: [student@fedora lab03]$ uniq fruits.txt banana apple cherry apple kiwi banana apple [student@fedora lab03]$ sort fruits.txt | uniq apple banana cherry kiwi [student@fedora lab03]$ sort fruits.txt | uniq -c 3 apple 2 banana 1 cherry 1 kiwi [student@fedora lab03]$ sort fruits.txt | uniq -c | sort -nr 3 apple 2 banana 1 kiwi 1 cherry [student@fedora lab03]$ sort fruits.txt | uniq -d apple banana uniq fruits.txt changed nothing: in fruits.txt, no line is the same as the one above it. After sort, the three apple lines are together, and uniq kept only one of them. -c wrote in front of every line how many times it appeared. sort -nr sorted these lines by the number in front of them (-n), from the largest (-r): the most frequent line is the first one. -d printed only the lines that appear more than once. Option What it does uniq -c Prints in front of every line how many times it appears (count) uniq -d Prints only the lines that appear more than once (duplicates) uniq -u Prints only the lines that appear exactly once (unique) uniq -i Ignores upper and lower case sort -n Sorts by the number at the beginning of the line, not alphabetically (10 after 9, not before) sort -r Sorts in reverse order sort -u Sorts and removes the repeated lines, the same as sort | uniq caution Without sort, uniq removes only the repeated lines that are next to each other. uniq fruits.txt still has three apple lines.

The kernel makes some special files in /dev. They are not stored on the disk: a driver in the kernel answers when a command reads or writes them. File Reading gives Writing Used for /dev/null nothing: end of file right away everything is discarded throwing away output you don't want: find /etc -name passwd 2> /dev/null /dev/zero bytes with the value 0, without end everything is discarded creating a file of a given size: head -c 1M /dev/zero > zeros.bin /dev/urandom random bytes, without end allowed, but not needed random data, keys and passwords: head -c 16 /dev/urandom | xxd [student@fedora lab03]$ find /etc -name passwd 2> /dev/null /etc/pam.d/passwd /etc/passwd [student@fedora lab03]$ head -c 8 /dev/zero | xxd 00000000: 0000 0000 0000 0000 ........ [student@fedora lab03]$ head -c 8 /dev/urandom | xxd 00000000: 9f3a 51c2 07e8 b4d1 .:Q..... 2> /dev/null threw away the Permission denied messages of find. head -c 8 kept the first 8 bytes, and xxd showed them in hexadecimal: zeros, then random bytes (different every time).

An archive is a single file that holds many files and directories, together with their names, their dates and their permissions. Compression makes a file smaller, by writing the same information with fewer bytes. On Linux, the two are usually done by different programs: tar makes the archive, and gzip, bzip2 or xz compress it. zip does both at once.

The three compressors work in the same way: they replace a file with a compressed one, with an extension added at the end, and they put it back when you decompress it. Compress Decompress Extension gzip <file> gunzip <file>.gz or gzip -d .gz the fastest, compresses the least bzip2 <file> bunzip2 <file>.bz2 or bzip2 -d .bz2 slower, compresses more xz <file> unxz <file>.xz or xz -d .xz the slowest, usually compresses the most Option Means (the same for all three) -k keep the original file -c write the result to the standard output, to use with > or |: the original is kept -v verbose: print how much smaller the file got -1 ... -9 from the fastest (-1) to the best compression (-9) [student@fedora lab03]$ gzip -k numbers.txt [student@fedora lab03]$ bzip2 -k numbers.txt [student@fedora lab03]$ xz -k numbers.txt [student@fedora lab03]$ ls -l numbers.txt* -rw-r--r--. 1 student student 108894 Oct 6 10:12 numbers.txt -rw-r--r--. 1 student student 25147 Oct 6 10:12 numbers.txt.bz2 -rw-r--r--. 1 student student 45016 Oct 6 10:12 numbers.txt.gz -rw-r--r--. 1 student student 4948 Oct 6 10:12 numbers.txt.xz [student@fedora lab03]$ rm numbers.txt [student@fedora lab03]$ unxz -k numbers.txt.xz [student@fedora lab03]$ wc -l numbers.txt 20000 numbers.txt With -k, each compressor kept numbers.txt and made a compressed copy of it. The same file became 45 KB with gzip, 25 KB with bzip2 and less than 5 KB with xz. After deleting numbers.txt, unxz -k put it back from numbers.txt.xz, with all its 20000 lines. caution Without -k, gzip numbers.txt deletes numbers.txt and leaves only numbers.txt.gz. This is the normal behavior of all three compressors. With -v, the three compressors print how well they compressed, but not in the same way: [student@fedora lab03]$ gzip -v -k numbers.txt numbers.txt: 58.7% -- created numbers.txt.gz [student@fedora lab03]$ bzip2 -v -k numbers.txt numbers.txt: 4.330:1, 1.847 bits/byte, 76.91% saved, 108894 in, 25147 out. [student@fedora lab03]$ xz -v -k numbers.txt numbers.txt (1/1) 100 % 4,948 B / 106.3 KiB = 0.045 Compressor Prints Better compression means gzip -v how much it saved, as a percentage: 58.7% a larger percentage bzip2 -v how much it saved (76.91% saved), and the sizes before (in) and after (out) a larger percentage xz -v the new size, the old size and the ratio between them: 0.045 means the new file is 4.5% of the old one, so 95.5% was saved a smaller ratio The 100 % that xz prints is not the compression: it is how much of the file it has read so far, and it always ends at 100 %. info A compressor works on one file. It cannot put a directory or several files together: this is the job of tar.

documents.t: tar (tape archive) puts files and directories together into a single file, usually called .tar. Its options are letters, written together, and the most used ones are: Letter Long form Means c --create create an archive t --list list the content of an archive x --extract extract an archive r --append add files at the end of an archive (not for compressed archives) v --verbose verbose: print the name of every file f <archive> --file <archive> the name of the archive file -C <directory> --directory <directory> change to directory first: extract the archive there, or take the files from there tip Every tar command has exactly one of c, t, x and r: what to do. The other letters change how it is done. The letters are written together, without a - (tar cvf, the old style, or tar -cvf). Put f last: the word right after the letters is the name of the archive. -C is written apart, with its own -. Command What it does tar cvf music.tar Music fruits.txt Creates music.tar with the directory Music, everything inside it, and the file fruits.txt tar tf music.tar Lists the content of music.tar tar tvf music.tar Lists the content with the details: permissions, owner, size and date tar xvf music.tar Extracts music.tar in the current directory tar xvf music.tar -C /tmp/extract Extracts it in /tmp/extract (the directory must exist) tar xvf music.tar Music/jazz.mp3 Extracts only one file, with the name it has in the archive tar rvf music.tar numbers.txt Adds numbers.txt at the end of the archive caution tar x overwrites the files that already exist, without asking. Extract into an empty directory with -C when you are not sure what is in the archive. [student@fedora lab03]$ tar cvf music.tar Music fruits.txt Music/ Music/jazz.mp3 Music/pop.mp3 Music/rock.mp3 fruits.txt [student@fedora lab03]$ tar tf music.tar Music/ Music/jazz.mp3 Music/pop.mp3 Music/rock.mp3 fruits.txt [student@fedora lab03]$ mkdir /tmp/extract [student@fedora lab03]$ tar xvf music.tar -C /tmp/extract Music/ Music/jazz.mp3 Music/pop.mp3 Music/rock.mp3 fruits.txt [student@fedora lab03]$ file music.tar music.tar: POSIX tar archive (GNU) tar cvf created the archive and printed every file it put in it, the directory Music with everything inside it. tar tf listed the content without extracting anything. tar xvf ... -C /tmp/extract recreated the same files in /tmp/extract: /tmp/extract/Music/jazz.mp3, and so on. file looked inside the archive and found that it is a tar archive. caution Do not forget the name of the archive after f. tar cvf Music tries to create an archive called Music and stops with Cowardly refusing to create an empty archive. Worse, tar cvf fruits.txt Music overwrites fruits.txt with an archive. info A .tar archive is not compressed. It is as large as all its files together, plus a little: for every file and directory, tar adds 512 bytes with its name, permissions, owner and date, and it fills the end of every file up to a multiple of 512 bytes.

tar can compress the archive, with one more letter. It runs gzip, bzip2 or xz for you: Letter Compressor Extension Example z gzip .tar.gz or .tgz tar czvf music.tar.gz Music j bzip2 .tar.bz2 or .tbz2 tar cjvf music.tar.bz2 Music J xz .tar.xz or .txz tar cJvf music.tar.xz Music To list or extract a compressed archive, you do not need the letter: tar finds out the compression by itself. [student@fedora lab03]$ tar cf all.tar Music numbers.txt [student@fedora lab03]$ tar czf all.tar.gz Music numbers.txt [student@fedora lab03]$ tar cjf all.tar.bz2 Music numbers.txt [student@fedora lab03]$ tar cJf all.tar.xz Music numbers.txt [student@fedora lab03]$ ls -l all.* -rw-r--r--. 1 student student 112640 Oct 6 10:20 all.tar -rw-r--r--. 1 student student 25333 Oct 6 10:20 all.tar.bz2 -rw-r--r--. 1 student student 45234 Oct 6 10:20 all.tar.gz -rw-r--r--. 1 student student 5692 Oct 6 10:20 all.tar.xz [student@fedora lab03]$ file all.* all.tar: POSIX tar archive (GNU) all.tar.bz2: bzip2 compressed data, block size = 900k all.tar.gz: gzip compressed data, from Unix, original size modulo 2^32 112640 all.tar.xz: XZ compressed data, checksum CRC64 [student@fedora lab03]$ tar tvf all.tar.xz drwxr-xr-x student/student 0 2026-10-06 10:12 Music/ -rw-r--r-- student/student 0 2026-10-06 10:12 Music/jazz.mp3 -rw-r--r-- student/student 0 2026-10-06 10:12 Music/pop.mp3 -rw-r--r-- student/student 0 2026-10-06 10:12 Music/rock.mp3 -rw-r--r-- student/student 108894 2026-10-06 10:12 numbers.txt The four archives hold the same files. The .tar is a little larger than the files themselves; the compressed ones are much smaller, xz the smallest. file recognized every type from the content, not from the extension. tar tvf listed the .tar.xz archive without being told it is compressed with xz. tip A compressed archive is a .tar archive compressed as a single file: all.tar.gz is exactly what you get with tar cf all.tar ... followed by gzip all.tar. This is why it has two extensions.

zip archives and compresses in one step, and its archives open on every operating system, including Windows and macOS. Command What it does zip music.zip Music/* Creates music.zip with the files in Music zip -r music.zip Music fruits.txt Creates music.zip with the directory Music, everything inside it, and fruits.txt zip -u music.zip numbers.txt Adds numbers.txt to the archive, or updates it if it changed zip -sf music.zip Lists the names in the archive unzip -l music.zip Lists the content, with sizes and dates unzip music.zip Extracts the archive in the current directory unzip music.zip -d /tmp/unzipped Extracts it in /tmp/unzipped (the directory is created) unzip music.zip fruits.txt Extracts only one file info When zip is given an archive name, it creates the archive if it doesn’t exist. If the archive already exists, zip updates it: files not yet in the archive are added, files with the same path are replaced, and all other existing entries are left unchanged. [student@fedora lab03]$ zip -r music.zip Music fruits.txt adding: Music/ (stored 0%) adding: Music/jazz.mp3 (stored 0%) adding: Music/pop.mp3 (stored 0%) adding: Music/rock.mp3 (stored 0%) adding: fruits.txt (deflated 40%) [student@fedora lab03]$ unzip -l music.zip Archive: music.zip Length Date Time Name --------- ---------- ----- ---- 0 10-06-2026 10:12 Music/ 0 10-06-2026 10:12 Music/jazz.mp3 0 10-06-2026 10:12 Music/pop.mp3 0 10-06-2026 10:12 Music/rock.mp3 44 10-06-2026 10:12 fruits.txt --------- ------- 44 5 files zip printed how much it compressed every file: the empty .mp3 files were stored as they are, and fruits.txt became 40% smaller. caution Without -r, zip music.zip Music puts only the empty directory in the archive, not the files inside it. info zip creates music.zip only if it does not exist yet. If the archive already exists, zip adds to it the files that are not in it, and replaces the ones that have the same name (it prints updating: instead of adding: for them). The files that are already in the archive stay there. To start from an empty archive, delete the old one first.

Format Archive and compress with Extract with Use it for .tar tar cf tar xf putting files together, without compressing them .tar.gz tar czf tar xf the most common archive on Linux, fast .tar.bz2 tar cjf tar xf smaller archives, older programs .tar.xz tar cJf tar xf the smallest archives, for example the source code of the Linux kernel .zip zip -r unzip files you send to people who use Windows or macOS tip Not sure what an archive is? Run file on it. The extension is only part of the name: file looks at the content.

A program is a file on the disk, for example /usr/bin/sleep. When you run it, the operating system loads it into memory and it becomes a process. Every process has a number, the PID (Process ID), and remembers the PID of the process that started it, its parent: the PPID (Parent Process ID).

Command What it shows echo $$ The PID of the current shell ps The processes of the current terminal ps -f The same processes, with more columns: UID, PID, PPID, the start time and the full command ps -e All the processes of the system (every process) ps -ef All the processes of the system, with the columns of -f ps -p <PID> Only the process with this PID ps -o <columns> Only the columns you choose, for example ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd ps --no-headers Without the first line, the one with the names of the columns pgrep <name> Only the PIDs of the processes whose name contains name The columns that ps prints, and the names you give to -o to choose them: Column Name for -o What it shows UID or USER user The user that owns the process PID pid The number of the process PPID ppid The number of its parent C c How much of the processor it uses, as a percentage STIME stime When it started TTY tty The terminal it runs in (pts/0, pts/1, ...); ? for the processes that have no terminal TIME time How much processor time it has used so far, not how long it has been running STAT stat Its state: S, R, T or Z, from the table of states below, followed by some details (for example s for the first process of a session, like a shell, and + for a process that runs in the foreground of its terminal) CMD cmd The full command line, with its parameters COMMAND comm Only the name of the program, without its parameters [student@fedora ~]$ ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd PID PPID STAT CMD 2817 2790 Ss bash 3110 2817 R+ ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd The shell, bash, waits for a command (S) and is the first process of its session (s). ps runs (R) in the foreground of the terminal (+), and its parent is bash. [student@fedora ~]$ echo $$ 2817 [student@fedora ~]$ ps -f UID PID PPID C STIME TTY TIME CMD student 2817 2790 0 10:02 pts/0 00:00:00 bash student 3105 2817 0 10:15 pts/0 00:00:00 ps -f The shell of this terminal is bash, with the PID 2817, the same number as $$. ps is a process too, started by bash: its PPID is 2817. Every time you run it, it gets a new PID. To have a process to look at, open a second terminal and start a command that keeps running, for example sleep 1000 (it waits for 1000 seconds). Find it from the first terminal: [student@fedora ~]$ pgrep sleep 3150 [student@fedora ~]$ ps -f -p 3150 UID PID PPID C STIME TTY TIME CMD student 3150 2905 0 10:16 pts/1 00:00:00 sleep 1000 sleep runs in the other terminal (pts/1), and its parent, 2905, is the bash of that terminal. When you are done with it, stop it with Ctrl+C in its terminal.

The kernel shows every process as a directory in /proc, named after its PID, for example for the sleep above it will be /proc/3150. Like the special files, these files are not on the disk: the kernel makes up their content when you read them. /proc/self is always the directory of the process that reads it, and /proc/$$ is the one of your shell. File What it shows /proc/<PID>/status The name, the state, the PID, the PPID, the owner and the memory of the process /proc/<PID>/cmdline The command line, with the words separated by \0 bytes instead of spaces /proc/<PID>/cwd A link to the current directory of the process /proc/<PID>/exe A link to the program that runs /proc/<PID>/fd/ The File Descriptor Table: one link for every open file /proc/<PID>/environ The environment variables, separated by \0 bytes /proc/<PID>/maps How the program and its libraries are placed in memory [student@fedora ~]$ head -n 7 /proc/3150/status Name: sleep Umask: 0022 State: S (sleeping) Tgid: 3150 Ngid: 0 Pid: 3150 PPid: 2905 [student@fedora ~]$ ls -l /proc/3150/exe /proc/3150/cwd lrwxrwxrwx. 1 student student 0 Oct 6 10:17 /proc/3150/cwd -> /home/student lrwxrwxrwx. 1 student student 0 Oct 6 10:17 /proc/3150/exe -> /usr/bin/sleep [student@fedora ~]$ cat -v /proc/3150/cmdline sleep^@1000^@ [student@fedora ~]$ ls -l /proc/3150/fd total 0 lrwx------. 1 student student 64 Oct 6 10:17 0 -> /dev/pts/1 lrwx------. 1 student student 64 Oct 6 10:17 1 -> /dev/pts/1 lrwx------. 1 student student 64 Oct 6 10:17 2 -> /dev/pts/1 status shows that sleep is waiting (S), and that its parent is 2905. exe points to the program, /usr/bin/sleep, and cwd to the directory where it was started. cmdline separates the words with \0 bytes, which are invisible: cat -v shows them as ^@. 0, 1 and 2 point to /dev/pts/1: the second terminal, which is both its keyboard and its display. The letter in the State line (and in the STAT column of ps) is the state of the process: Letter State Means R Running or Ready Runs on a processor, or waits for one S Sleeping (waiting) Waits for something: a key, a timer, data from a pipe T Stopped Paused, for example with Ctrl+Z Z Zombie Finished, but its parent has not read its exit code yet /proc also has files about the whole system: File What it shows /proc/cpuinfo The processors, one block for each of them /proc/meminfo The memory, in kB: MemTotal, MemFree, MemAvailable, ... /proc/uptime Two numbers: the seconds since the system started, then the seconds the processors were idle (added up for all of them) /proc/loadavg The load in the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes, then the processes that are now in the Running state / all processes, and the last PID given /proc/version The version of the kernel, and the compiler that built it info The PIDs and the paths above are different on your computer: use the ones that pgrep and ps print for you. You can read the files of your own processes; for the processes of other users, most of them say Permission denied.

top shows the processes live, like the Task Manager of Windows. It updates the list every few seconds, with the processes that use the most processor time at the top. top - 10:30:12 up 1:28, 1 user, load average: 0.08, 0.12, 0.10 Tasks: 248 total, 1 running, 247 sleeping, 0 stopped, 0 zombie %Cpu(s): 1.3 us, 0.7 sy, 0.0 ni, 97.9 id, 0.0 wa, 0.1 hi, 0.0 si, 0.0 st MiB Mem : 3911.4 total, 1873.2 free, 1245.6 used, 1042.9 buff/cache MiB Swap: 3911.0 total, 3911.0 free, 0.0 used. 2665.8 avail Mem PID USER PR NI VIRT RES SHR S %CPU %MEM TIME+ COMMAND 1718 student 20 0 1186420 98340 61200 S 1.3 2.5 0:12.41 sway 2790 student 20 0 318264 41212 30124 S 0.3 1.0 0:02.03 foot 1 root 20 0 49736 38544 10208 S 0.0 1.0 0:02.31 systemd The first lines are a summary of the system: the time since it started, the load, how many processes are in every state, the use of the processors and of the memory. Below, every process has its PID, its owner (USER), its memory (RES, in KB), its state (S), the share of the processor and of the memory it uses, and its command. Key Action P Sort by processor use (the default) M Sort by memory use T Sort by the processor time used so far c Show the full command line u Show only the processes of a user (type the name and press Enter) 1 Show every processor on its own line V Show the processes as a tree h Help q Quit tip top -b -n 1 prints the list only once, without updating it, so you can redirect it: top -b -n 1 > top.txt.

htop does the same job as top, but with colors, bars for every processor, and menus at the bottom of the screen. Start it with htop and quit with q or F10. At the top, htop shows a bar for every processor (0 and 1), the memory (Mem) and the swap (Swp), the number of tasks, the load average and the uptime. Below them is the list of processes, one per line, and at the bottom the menu with the function keys. In the image above, the list shows only the processes of student (u) as a tree (F5): the terminal (foot) runs four bash shells, and each of them runs a command (the third one runs the pipeline sleep 800 | sleep 900). The chosen process is sleep 1000. Key Action Like ↑ ↓ Choose a process F3 or / Search: jump to the next process whose command contains a text (press again for the next one) pgrep F4 or \ Filter: show only the processes whose command contains a text (Esc shows all again) F5 or t Show the processes as a tree V in top F6 Choose the column to sort by P / M Sort by processor use / memory use / processor time P / M in top u Show only the processes of a user, chosen from a list u in top l Show the open files of the chosen process ls -l /proc/<PID>/fd F2 Setup: choose the columns and the colors F1 or h Help q or F10 Quit tip htop also shows the threads of the processes, in green. Press H to hide them and the list becomes much shorter.

btop is a newer program of the same kind. Its screen is split into boxes: the processors with a graph of their use, the memory and the disks, the network, and the list of processes. Start it with btop and quit with q. Key Action ↑ ↓ Choose a process Enter Show the details of the chosen process f or / Show only the processes that match a text (filter) e Show the processes as a tree ← → Choose the column to sort by r Reverse the sorting order 1 ... 4 Show or hide the boxes: processors, memory, network, processes Esc or m Menu h or F1 Help q Quit

Problem Solution bash: <command>: command not found The program is not installed: install it with sudo dnf install <package> on Fedora, or with sudo apt install <package> on Debian and Ubuntu; the package usually has the same name as the command The error still shows on the display after > Errors go to 2: use 2> or &> A file is empty after a redirect > empties the file first: use >> to append A command waits and does nothing It reads from the keyboard: type the input and press Ctrl+D, or stop it with Ctrl+C gzip: numbers.txt.gz already exists The compressed file is already there: delete it, or add -f to overwrite it The original file disappeared after gzip Normal: use -k to keep it, or decompress it with gunzip tar: Cowardly refusing to create an empty archive The name of the archive after f is missing tar: ...: Not found in archive The name is wrong: list the archive with tar tf and copy the name exactly tar: /tmp/extract: Cannot open: No such file or directory The directory given to -C must exist: create it with mkdir A zip archive has a directory, but not its files Add -r No such file or directory in /proc/<PID> The process has finished, or the PID is wrong: check it with pgrep or ps Permission denied in /proc/<PID> The process belongs to another user

The exercises get harder as you go: 🧪 First Steps (exercises 1 - 32) goes once through everything in this lab, with easy exercises; 🏠 Going Further (exercises 33 - 47) has harder exercises; 📝 Challenges (exercises 48 - 54) has the hardest ones. Exercise 1 creates the files and directories that all the other exercises start from; any other file an exercise needs, it creates by itself. Run the commands in ~/lab03, unless the exercise says otherwise. If you change or delete one of the files from exercise 1, run its commands again to get it back. Some exercises ask for things that the lab does not show you, for example an option that is not in the tables above. Find it in the manual page of the command (man <command>), as explained in Searching in a Manual Page in lab 02. Many exercises use the files of the system, from /etc, /usr, /var, /proc and /dev, so that you also get to know how a Linux system is organized. To find out what a directory is for, look in man hier; to find out what a file in /etc contains, look in section 5 of the manual, for example man 5 passwd, man 5 shells or man 5 os-release. Keep two terminals side by side in Sway: the first one to run the commands, and the second one to run the commands that you inspect, or to check the results. Many exercises use the PID of a process: it is different on your computer, use the one that pgrep or ps prints for you. danger Do not use sudo to look at processes. The files in /proc are made by the kernel: read them, but do not try to change them.

Check: you see the four directories, the five empty files, fruits.txt and numbers.txt; wc -l prints 7 and 20000. → Navigation Redirects The root of the system: save the tree of /, only one level deep, into Reports/system.txt (look in man tree for the option that limits how deep tree goes); print Reports/system.txt with cat. Check: tree printed nothing on the display, and the file shows the main directories of the system: boot, dev, etc, home, proc, tmp, usr and var; bin is a link to usr/bin. → Output Append and overwrite: save the tree of /usr, one level deep, into Reports/tree.txt; append the tree of /var, one level deep, to Reports/tree.txt, and print the file; overwrite Reports/tree.txt with the tree of /home, one level deep, and print the file again. Check: after the append, the file has both trees: /usr with bin, lib and share, then /var with cache, lib and log; after the overwrite, it has only the tree of /home, with student. → Output Errors apart: with a single ls -a command, list /etc/skel (the files copied into the home directory of every new user) and /root (the home directory of the administrator), so that the list goes into Reports/list.txt and the error into Reports/errors.txt; print the content of the two files. Check: nothing appears on the display when you run ls; Reports/list.txt has, among others, .bashrc and .bash_profile, and Reports/errors.txt has a Permission denied for /root. → Errors Append errors: run ls /root and save its error into Reports/errors.txt, overwriting the file; print /etc/shadow (the file with the passwords of the users) with cat, and append its error to Reports/errors.txt; print the content Reports/errors.txt. Check: Reports/errors.txt has two lines, one for /root and one for /etc/shadow: only root can read them. → Errors The users and the groups: copy /etc/passwd (the list of the users) into Reports/users.txt without cp: print it with cat and redirect the output into the new file; copy /etc/group (the list of the groups) into Reports/groups.txt in the same way; count the lines of the two copies and of the two originals with wc -l. Check: every copy has the same number of lines as its original. → Output Everything in one file: run ls -a /etc/skel /root so that both the list and the error go into Reports/all.txt, using &>, and print the file; run the same command again, this time with the older way, > Reports/all.txt 2>&1 (see the table of redirects), and print the file again. Check: both times, Reports/all.txt has the error for /root and the files of /etc/skel, and nothing appears on the display when you run ls. → Redirects Silence: search /etc and /usr for files called os-release with find, and throw the errors away so that you do not see any Permission denied message; print the content of /etc/os-release (the file that describes your distribution) with cat. Check: find prints only two paths, /etc/os-release and /usr/lib/os-release; /etc/os-release has the name and the version of your distribution, Fedora Linux. → Special Files Input from a file: sort /etc/shells (the list of the shells installed in the system) with sort, giving it the file with <; count the lines of /etc/passwd with wc -l, giving it the name of the file as a parameter; count them again, this time giving the file with <. Check: the shells in /bin come before the ones in /usr/bin; both counts are the same, but only the first wc prints the name of the file. → Input Type a file: run cat with a redirect, so that what you type goes into Reports/todo.txt; type three lines, then press Ctrl+D at the beginning of a new line to end the input; print the content of Reports/todo.txt. Check: cat Reports/todo.txt prints the three lines you typed. → Input Pipes: count the programs in /usr/bin with ls, wc -l and a pipe; count the files and directories in /etc (the configuration of the system) that ls shows, in the same way; show the long list of /etc (ls -l) on one screen at a time, with less. Check: there are more than a thousand programs and a few hundred entries in /etc; less stops after every screen, and you quit it with q. → Pipes Search with grep: show the line of your user, student, from /etc/passwd (the list of the users); count the lines of /etc/passwd that contain nologin: these are the users of the services, which cannot log in; list the programs in /usr/bin whose name contains zip. Check: your line ends with /home/student:/bin/bash; most of the users have nologin; the list of programs has gzip and gunzip. → Searching for a Text Repeated lines: run uniq fruits.txt and find out why it does not remove anything; print every fruit from fruits.txt only once; print every fruit with the number of times it appears, the most frequent first; print only the fruits that appear exactly once (look in man uniq). Check: uniq fruits.txt prints the same 7 lines; after sort, you get 4 fruits, 3 apple is the first line of the count, and only cherry and kiwi appear exactly once. → Repeated Lines Zeros and random bytes: show the first 16 bytes of /dev/zero in hexadecimal, with head and xxd; show the first 16 bytes of /dev/urandom in the same way, and run the command twice. Check: the bytes of /dev/zero are all zeros; the bytes of /dev/urandom are different every time you run the command. → Special Files Processes My shell: print the PID of your shell; list the processes of the terminal with all the columns of -f; show only the Name, State, Pid and PPid lines of the /proc/$$/status file of your shell: give grep every text after its own -e (grep -e Name -e State ...), and look in man grep for the option that matches only whole words, so that Pid does not also match TracerPid. Check: ps and status show the same PID and PPID for bash, and its state is S. → Listing Processes · The /proc File System Inspect a process: in the second terminal, run sleep 1000; in the first terminal, find the PID of sleep with pgrep; print its /proc/<PID>/status file; print its command line, from /proc/<PID>/cmdline, with cat -v; find out its program and its current directory, from the links /proc/<PID>/exe and /proc/<PID>/cwd; stop sleep with Ctrl+C in the second terminal. Check: the state is S, the command line is sleep^@1000^@, the program is /usr/bin/sleep, and the current directory is the one you were in when you ran sleep (run pwd in the second terminal to compare). → The /proc File System Open files: list the File Descriptor Table of your shell, from /proc/$$/fd; in the second terminal, run sleep 1000; in the first terminal, find the PID of sleep and list its File Descriptor Table; stop sleep with Ctrl+C and try to list its table again. Check: 0, 1 and 2 point to a /dev/pts/... file, a different one for each terminal (bash also keeps 255 open on the same terminal, for its own use); after Ctrl+C, /proc/<PID> no longer exists. → The /proc File System The system: Find out about your computer using only the files in /proc: the model of the processor: the model name lines of /proc/cpuinfo (use grep); how many processors you have: count the processor lines of /proc/cpuinfo; the total memory: the MemTotal line of /proc/meminfo; for how many seconds the system has been running: the first number in /proc/uptime; the version of the kernel: /proc/version. Check: the number of processors is the same as the one printed by nproc, the time matches the up part of uptime, and the version of the kernel is the same as uname -r. → The /proc File System top and htop: start top, sort the processes by memory, then by processor, and quit; start htop, search for bash and press F3 until the chosen line is the bash of the first terminal (the PID printed by echo $$), show the processes as a tree, and quit. Check: top shows the Tasks line with the number of processes in every state; in the tree of htop, your bash is under the terminal. → top · htop Archives and compression Three compressors: delete numbers.txt.gz, numbers.txt.bz2 and numbers.txt.xz, if they exist; compress numbers.txt with gzip, with bzip2 and with xz, keeping the original file every time; compare the sizes of the four files with ls -l. Check: you have numbers.txt, numbers.txt.gz, numbers.txt.bz2 and numbers.txt.xz, and the .xz file is the smallest. → Compressing One File How much smaller: delete numbers.txt.gz, numbers.txt.bz2 and numbers.txt.xz, if they exist; compress numbers.txt with gzip, with bzip2 and with xz, keeping the original file, so that each of them prints how much smaller the file got (look in their manual pages for the option that prints more details). Check: gzip and bzip2 printed how much they saved, as a percentage, and the one of bzip2 is larger; xz printed a ratio instead (about 0.045, the new size divided by the old one), so it saved about 95%, the most of the three. → Compressing One File Decompress: delete numbers.txt.gz and numbers.txt.bz2, if they exist; compress numbers.txt with gzip, without keeping the original, and check with ls that numbers.txt is gone; get numbers.txt back from numbers.txt.gz; compress numbers.txt with bzip2, keeping the original, then delete numbers.txt; get numbers.txt back from numbers.txt.bz2, this time keeping the compressed file. Check: wc -l numbers.txt prints 20000 both times; numbers.txt.gz is gone (gunzip deleted it, like gzip deletes the original), but numbers.txt.bz2 still exists. → Compressing One File What kind of file: delete numbers.txt.bz2 and numbers.txt.xz, if they exist; compress numbers.txt with bzip2 and with xz, keeping the original; find out the types of numbers.txt, numbers.txt.bz2 and numbers.txt.xz, with a single file command; delete numbers.txt.bz2 and numbers.txt.xz; find out the type of /usr/share/man/man1/ls.1.gz, the manual page of ls. Check: file says ASCII text, bzip2 compressed data and XZ compressed data, and gzip compressed data for ls.1.gz: the manual pages are stored compressed with gzip, and man decompresses them when you read them. → Which One to Use A tar archive: create Archives/music.tar with the directories Music and Photos and the file fruits.txt; list the content of the archive; find out the type of the archive with file. Check: the archive has Music/, Photos/, the five empty files and fruits.txt, and file says POSIX tar archive. → Archives Extract: create Archives/music.tar with Music, Photos and fruits.txt (if it already exists, tar overwrites it); create the directory /tmp/extract with mkdir -p, so that there is no error if it already exists; extract Archives/music.tar into /tmp/extract. Check: tree /tmp/extract shows Music, Photos and fruits.txt, with the same files as in ~/lab03. → Archives Only one file: create Archives/music.tar with Music, Photos and fruits.txt; create the directory /tmp/single with mkdir -p, so that there is no error if it already exists; extract only Photos/dog.jpg from Archives/music.tar into /tmp/single. Check: tree /tmp/single shows Photos/dog.jpg, and nothing else. → Archives Add a file: create Archives/music.tar with Music, Photos and fruits.txt; add numbers.txt to Archives/music.tar, without creating the archive again; list the archive with the details of every file. Check: numbers.txt is the last file in the list, with the size 108894. → Archives Compressed archives: create Archives/all.tar with Music, Photos and numbers.txt; create Archives/all.tar.gz, Archives/all.tar.bz2 and Archives/all.tar.xz, each with the same three entries, compressed with gzip, bzip2 and xz; compare the sizes of the four archives with ls -l. Check: the .tar is the largest and the .tar.xz the smallest. → Compressed Archives List compressed archives: create Archives/all.tar.gz, Archives/all.tar.bz2 and Archives/all.tar.xz, each with Music, Photos and numbers.txt; list the content of each archive, without telling tar how it is compressed; find out the types of the three archives with file. Check: all three lists are the same; file shows a different compression for each of them. → Compressed Archives Extract compressed archives: create Archives/all.tar.gz, Archives/all.tar.bz2 and Archives/all.tar.xz, each with Music, Photos and numbers.txt; create the directories /tmp/gz, /tmp/bz2 and /tmp/xz; extract each archive into its own directory: the .tar.gz into /tmp/gz, the .tar.bz2 into /tmp/bz2 and the .tar.xz into /tmp/xz; show the three directories with tree. Check: the trees of the three directories are the same. → Compressed Archives A zip archive: delete Archives/all.zip, if it exists (zip would update it, not create it again); create Archives/all.zip with Music, Photos and numbers.txt, with everything inside the directories; list the content of the archive; extract it into /tmp/unzipped. Check: unzip -l lists 8 entries, and tree /tmp/unzipped shows Music with three files, Photos with two files, and numbers.txt. → Zip Archives Update a zip archive: delete Archives/all.zip, if it exists; create Archives/all.zip with Music, Photos and numbers.txt, with everything inside the directories; add fruits.txt to Archives/all.zip; list the files in the archive with zip -sf; extract only fruits.txt from the archive into /tmp/fruit. Check: zip -sf Archives/all.zip lists fruits.txt as the last file, and /tmp/fruit has only fruits.txt. → Zip Archives

Order matters: run ls /etc/skel /root > Reports/a.txt 2>&1 and print Reports/a.txt; run ls /etc/skel /root 2>&1 > Reports/b.txt and print Reports/b.txt; find out why the error is in a.txt, but not in b.txt. Check: the second command printed the error on the display, and Reports/b.txt has only the list of /etc/skel. Hint: the shell reads the redirects from left to right. → Redirects See and save: In a single command line, save the list of the programs in /usr/bin into Reports/programs.txt and count them (look in man tee for the command that writes its input both to a file and to its output). Check: the number printed is the same as wc -l < Reports/programs.txt. → Pipes Redirects seen from inside: in the second terminal, run sleep 900 < ~/lab03/fruits.txt > /tmp/out.txt 2> /dev/null; in the first terminal, find the PID of sleep and list its File Descriptor Table; stop sleep with Ctrl+C in the second terminal. Check: 0 points to fruits.txt, 1 to /tmp/out.txt and 2 to /dev/null: the shell changed the table before sleep started. → The /proc File System · Redirects A pipe seen from inside: in the second terminal, run sleep 800 | sleep 900; in the first terminal, find the PIDs of the two sleep processes (look in man pgrep for the option that also prints the command line, so you can tell them apart); list the File Descriptor Tables of both processes; stop them with Ctrl+C in the second terminal. Check: 1 of sleep 800 and 0 of sleep 900 point to the same pipe:[...], with the same number. → The /proc File System · Pipes What does less read: in the second terminal, open /etc/services (the list of the network services and their ports) with less; in the first terminal, find the PID of less; list the files that less has open, and print its command line and its current directory, using /proc; quit less with q. Check: besides 0, 1 and 2, less has /etc/services open, at file descriptor 3 or higher. → The /proc File System Where is the other shell: in the second terminal, go to ~/lab03/Music and print the PID of the shell; in the first terminal, find the current directory of that shell, using /proc; open its environ file with less and find the value of the HOME variable: less warns that it may be a binary file, because of the \0 bytes between the variables, so answer y; the \0 bytes show up as ^@, and you search with /. Check: cwd points to /home/student/lab03/Music, and environ has HOME=/home/student. → The /proc File System Save top: run top so that it prints its list only once and does not update it (see the tip in top); keep only the first 15 lines of its output, and save them into Reports/top.txt, in the same command line. Check: Reports/top.txt has 15 lines, starting with the summary of top. → top · Pipes htop in depth: In htop: hide the threads; show only your processes; sort them by memory; choose the bash of the first terminal (the PID printed by echo $$) and show its open files (if htop says that it cannot run lsof, install it with sudo dnf install lsof); add the PPID column: press F2, go to Screens, choose PPID in Available Columns, press Enter to add it, then leave the menu with F10. Check: the open files of bash are the same as in ls -l /proc/$$/fd, and the PPID of bash is the PID of the terminal. → htop Whose processes: count the processes of root with ps, wc -l and a pipe (look in man ps for the option that selects the processes of a user, and use --no-headers, so that wc -l does not also count the line with the names of the columns); count your own processes in the same way; count them again, without --no-headers. Check: root has many more processes than student: most of the system runs as root. Without --no-headers, each number is larger by one. → Listing Processes · Pipes Who runs the processes: list all the processes of the system with ps, printing only the column of the user, without the header line; in the same command line, using sort and uniq, print every user only once, with the number of its processes in front of it, the user with the most processes first. Check: the first line is root, with the same number as ps -u root --no-headers | wc -l, and student is among the first lines; the numbers added up are the same as ps -e --no-headers | wc -l. Some users may show up as numbers instead of names: ps prints the UID when the name is too long for the column. → Listing Processes · Repeated Lines Big files: create Archives/zeros.bin with the first 10 MB of /dev/zero, using head (look in man head for the option that prints a number of bytes instead of lines); create Archives/random.bin with the first 10 MB of /dev/urandom, in the same way; compress both files with xz, keeping the originals; compare the sizes of the four files with ls -lh; delete the four files: they are big. Check: zeros.bin.xz is a few KB, random.bin.xz is still about 10 MB: random data cannot be compressed. → Special Files · Compressing One File Compress into another file: Compress /etc/services (the list of the network services) without copying it and without changing /etc: use the option -c, which writes the compressed data to the standard output, and a redirect. compress it with gzip into Archives/services.gz; compress it with bzip2 into Archives/services.bz2; compress it with xz into Archives/services.xz; put time in front of each of the three commands, and compare the times and the sizes of the files. Check: the three files exist, /etc/services is unchanged, xz makes the smallest file and takes the longest. → Compressing One File Read without extracting: Look in man gzip and man xz for the commands that print the content of a compressed file, without creating any new file. compress /etc/services with gzip -c into Archives/services.gz, and with xz -c into Archives/services.xz; print the content of Archives/services.gz one screen at a time, with less; count the lines of Archives/services.xz; print the first 20 lines of the compressed manual page /usr/share/man/man1/ls.1.gz. Check: the count is the same as wc -l < /etc/services; the manual page is a text file with formatting commands, lines that start with ., like .TH and .SH. → Compressing One File Compression from the name: create Archives/photos.tar.bz2 with Photos, without telling tar the compressor: let it choose the compressor from the extension of the archive (look in man tar for this option); find out the type of the archive with file. Check: file Archives/photos.tar.bz2 says bzip2 compressed data. → Compressed Archives Without the full path: create /tmp/doc.tar.gz with the directory /usr/share/doc/bash (the documentation of bash), so that the names in the archive start with bash/ and not with usr/share/doc/ (look in man tar for the option that changes the directory before adding the files); list the content of the archive. Check: tar tf /tmp/doc.tar.gz lists names that start with bash/. → Archives

Count with /proc: count the directories in /proc whose name is a number (a wildcard can have a range of characters: [0-9] matches one digit; see man 7 glob); count the processes of the system with ps -e --no-headers and wc -l; compare the two numbers. Check: the two numbers are almost the same: every process is a directory in /proc. → The /proc File System The shells of the users: Every line of /etc/passwd has 7 fields separated by :, and the last one is the shell of the user. print only the shell of every user (look in man cut for the options that choose the separator and keep only one field of every line); in the same command line, print every shell only once, with the number of users that have it, the most used first; print only the shells that are used by more than one user. Check: a nologin shell is the first line, with most of the users. You may see both /sbin/nologin and /usr/sbin/nologin: they are the same program (/sbin is a link to usr/sbin), but uniq compares only the text, so it counts them on separate lines. /bin/bash is used by root and student, and the numbers added up are the same as wc -l < /etc/passwd. → Repeated Lines · Pipes Who has the file open: in the second terminal, open /etc/hosts (the names of the computers that the system knows without asking the network) with less; in the first terminal, find the file descriptor that points to /etc/hosts, without using pgrep or ps: search /proc/*/fd with find (look in man find for the test that checks where a symbolic link points to), and throw away the Permission denied errors for the processes of other users; check with ps -p that the number in the path that find prints is the PID of less; quit less with q. Check: find prints a path like /proc/3402/fd/4, and ps -p 3402 shows less. → The /proc File System Back up the configuration: create /tmp/etc.tar.gz with the whole /etc directory (the configuration of the system), except /etc/pki, the directory with the certificates that the system uses to check secure connections, like the https:// websites (look in man tar for the option that leaves files out of the archive); in the same command, save the errors of tar into Reports/etc-errors.txt; count the entries in the archive, with tar tf and wc -l; count only the Permission denied lines in Reports/etc-errors.txt, with grep -c. Check: tar tf /tmp/etc.tar.gz lists etc/passwd and etc/os-release, but nothing from etc/pki. Reports/etc-errors.txt has a Permission denied for every file that only root can read, like /etc/shadow, and two more lines that are not about a file. The first one, tar: Removing leading `/' from member names, only tells you that tar saves /etc/passwd as etc/passwd, so that the archive can be extracted anywhere. The last one, tar: Exiting with failure status due to previous errors, only says that there were errors. This is why you count only the Permission denied lines. → Compressed Archives Strip a directory: create Archives/all.tar.gz with Music, Photos and numbers.txt; create the directory /tmp/flat; extract Archives/all.tar.gz into /tmp/flat so that the files of Music and Photos end up directly in /tmp/flat, without their directories (look in man tar for the option that removes directories from the beginning of the names). Check: tree /tmp/flat shows the five empty files directly under /tmp/flat, but not numbers.txt. --strip-components=1 removes the first part of every name: Music/jazz.mp3 becomes jazz.mp3, but numbers.txt is in the top directory of the archive, so nothing is left of its name, and tar does not extract it (the same happens to the names Music/ and Photos/). → Archives Archives through a pipe: create /tmp/music.tar.gz with the directory Music, in a single command line, so that tar writes the archive, not compressed, to its standard output (an archive file named - means the standard output), gzip compresses it in a pipe, and a redirect saves it; create the directory /tmp/piped; extract /tmp/music.tar.gz into /tmp/piped in another pipe: gunzip -c decompresses it to its standard output, and tar reads the archive from its standard input (an archive file named - means the standard input). Check: file /tmp/music.tar.gz says gzip compressed data, and tree /tmp/piped shows Music. → Pipes · Compressed Archives Clean up: With a single rm command, delete everything that the exercises create in /tmp, without any error for the ones you did not create (look in man rm): danger rm -rf does not ask anything, and what it deletes cannot be recovered. Read the command twice before you press Enter: a space in the wrong place, like rm -rf /tmp /extract instead of rm -rf /tmp/extract, deletes much more than you want. the directories /tmp/extract, /tmp/single, /tmp/gz, /tmp/bz2, /tmp/xz, /tmp/unzipped, /tmp/fruit, /tmp/flat and /tmp/piped; the files /tmp/out.txt, /tmp/doc.tar.gz, /tmp/etc.tar.gz and /tmp/music.tar.gz. Check: rm prints nothing, and ls /tmp no longer shows them. → Managing Files

Use the last 5 minutes of the lab to answer these questions together with your colleagues and the teaching assistant. There are no wrong answers for the last two. What are the file descriptors 0, 1 and 2, and where do they point to in a terminal? What is the difference between > and >>? And between > and 2>? Why does wc -l < file not print the name of the file? What is the difference between an archive and a compressed file? Why does a .tar.gz have two extensions? When would you use .tar.xz, and when .zip? What is the difference between a program and a process? What are the PID and the PPID? Where are the files in /proc stored? What can you find out about a process from /proc that ps does not show? When would you use top, and when htop or btop? Which redirect or archive format will you use most often?

The memory of a process: Print /proc/$$/maps with less. Find the lines of /usr/bin/bash and of libc.so.6: this is how the loader placed the program and its libraries in memory. → The /proc File System Zstandard: Fedora also has zstd, a newer compressor. Compress numbers.txt with it and compare the size and the time with gzip and xz; then create a .tar.zst archive (look in man tar for the option that compresses the archive with zstd). → Compressing One File Archive managers: Open an archive with yazi (lab 02): it shows the content of .tar.gz and .zip archives as a preview. → Yazi htop settings: Press F2 in htop and change the meters at the top of the screen. → htop

In the third lab you learned to redirect what a command reads and writes, and to inspect the processes of the system. In this lab you will look closer at the shell and at the terminal it runs in. You will run commands in the background, stop them and bring them back, and send them signals. You will set variables and see which of them reach the commands you start. At the end you will find out exactly what the shell does with a line of text before a command starts: how it splits it into words, what the quotes and the globs do, and how it finds the program to run. The most important idea of this lab is that the command never sees what you type. The shell reads the line, replaces the variables and the globs, removes the quotes, sets up the redirects, finds the program and only then starts it, with a list of words as its parameters.

Understand what a terminal, a pseudo terminal and a shell are, and use the virtual terminals Send signals to processes with kill command and with the keyboard, and handle a signal with trap Run commands in the background and manage them as jobs with &, jobs, fg, bg and kill %N See how the processes of a terminal are grouped in process groups and sessions, and keep a command running after the terminal closes with nohup Use shell variables and environment variables, with export, unset, printenv and env, and the special parameters $?, $$ and $! Split a command line into its parts: the assignments, the command, its parameters and the redirects Use quotes and \ to control how the shell splits words and replaces variables Select files with globs: *, ?, [...], [!...], ** and {...} Tell built-in commands from external ones with type, and understand how the shell searches the PATH

In the past, a computer was shared by many users. Each of them had a terminal: a keyboard and a screen (or a printer), without a processor, connected to the computer by a cable. These terminals were TeleTypes, and Linux still calls a terminal a TTY. The terminals only sent the keys to the computer and printed what it sent back: all the programs ran on the mainframe. Today, the kernel gives every program that runs in a terminal a terminal device, a special file in /dev. The program reads the keys from it and writes the text to it, through the file descriptors 0, 1 and 2. Device What it is In ps /dev/tty1, /dev/tty2, ... the virtual terminals of the kernel: each one uses the screen and the keyboard of the computer, one at a time tty1 /dev/pts/0, /dev/pts/1, ... the pseudo terminals: one for every terminal window or tab, and for every SSH connection pts/0 /dev/tty not a terminal of its own: a shortcut to the terminal of the process that opens it never: ps shows the real one

A computer today has one screen and one keyboard, but the kernel makes them look like several terminals: the virtual terminals. Each one works like one of the old terminals, with its own login and its own programs, but only one of them is on the screen at a time. The kernel shows only one of them at a time. On /dev/tty1 in the image above, agetty printed the login prompt, and after the login the shell of alice, bash, uses the same terminal. The graphical interface runs in one of the virtual terminals too, usually the first or the second one. Before you leave it, find out which one, so you know how to come back. Run this in a terminal in Sway: [student@fedora ~]$ loginctl show-session $XDG_SESSION_ID -p VTNr VTNr=2 loginctl asks systemd about your login session: here, Sway runs in the second virtual terminal, /dev/tty2. Ctrl+Alt+F<n> switches to the virtual terminal n: Keys Goes to Ctrl+Alt+F3 ... F6 a text mode terminal, /dev/tty3 ... /dev/tty6 Ctrl+Alt+F2 back to Sway, if VTNr is 2 (F1 if it is 1) In a text mode terminal, a program called agetty waits for a user. Log in with your user and password: login checks them and starts your shell, bash. fedora login: student Password: [student@fedora ~]$ tty /dev/tty3 [student@fedora ~]$ exit tty prints the name of the terminal of the shell: this time a virtual terminal, /dev/tty3. exit closes the shell and agetty waits for a new login. Ctrl+Alt+F2 goes back to Sway, with all your windows exactly as you left them: Sway kept running while you were away. caution In a VirtualBox virtual machine, Ctrl+Alt+F3 is caught by your own operating system, not by the virtual machine. Use Host+F3 instead (the Host key is usually the right Ctrl), and Host+F2 to go back. Other virtual machines have a menu to send these keys. tip If you do not know where Sway is, try Ctrl+Alt+F1 and F2. One of them is Sway; the other one shows a login screen or a text terminal.

The graphical interface, Xorg or Wayland (Sway is a Wayland compositor), takes over one of the virtual terminals and draws on the screen through the framebuffer of the kernel. In it, a terminal is a graphical application, a terminal emulator: foot, kitty, ptyxis, alacritty, ghostty, ... Each window of a terminal emulator asks the kernel for a pseudo terminal: it opens /dev/ptmx, and the kernel creates a new /dev/pts/<n>. A pseudo terminal has two ends. The terminal emulator keeps one end, the master, and reads and writes it like a file. The other end, the slave, is the file /dev/pts/<n>: it behaves exactly like a real terminal. When the emulator starts the shell, it redirects /dev/pts/<n> as the 0, 1 and 2 of the shell. The keys you press are written by the emulator into the master, and the shell reads them from the slave. What the shell writes into the slave comes out of the master, and the emulator draws it in its window. The shell does not know that there is a window: it only sees a terminal. [student@fedora ~]$ tty /dev/pts/0 [student@fedora ~]$ ps PID TTY TIME CMD 2817 pts/0 00:00:00 bash 3104 pts/0 00:00:00 ps [student@fedora ~]$ ls /dev/pts 0 1 ptmx [student@fedora ~]$ ls -l /proc/$$/fd/0 lrwx------. 1 student student 64 Oct 20 10:02 /proc/2817/fd/0 -> /dev/pts/0 This shell runs in the first terminal window, /dev/pts/0, and ps shows only the processes of this terminal. There are two windows open, so there are two pseudo terminals, 0 and 1. The standard input of the shell is the pseudo terminal, as you saw in lab 03. tip A pseudo terminal is a file: what you write into it appears in the window of that terminal. With two terminals, echo hello > /dev/pts/1 run in the first one writes hello in the second one.

A signal is a short message that the operating system sends to a process: a number, with a name that starts with SIG. When a signal arrives, the process stops what it is doing and runs the default action of the signal, or, if it has one, its own signal handler, and then continues. Default action What happens to the process Term it ends Core it ends and leaves a copy of its memory (a core dump), for debugging Stop it is paused, until it receives SIGCONT Cont it continues, if it was stopped; otherwise nothing happens Ign nothing, the signal is thrown away info On Fedora, the core dumps do not appear as files in the current directory: systemd-coredump keeps them. coredumpctl list shows them, the newest last. info On Fedora, the core dumps do not appear as files in the current directory: systemd-coredump keeps them. coredumpctl list shows them, the newest last. The signals you will use most often: Number Signal Default action Sent when Can be handled? 1 SIGHUP Term the terminal closed (hang up) yes 2 SIGINT Term you pressed Ctrl+C (interrupt) yes 3 SIGQUIT Core you pressed Ctrl+\ yes 9 SIGKILL Term someone wants the process to end now no 15 SIGTERM Term someone asks the process to end; the default of kill yes 18 SIGCONT Cont fg or bg continues a stopped job yes, but it continues anyway 19 SIGSTOP Stop someone wants the process to stop now no 20 SIGTSTP Stop you pressed Ctrl+Z yes 21 SIGTTIN Stop a background process tried to read from the terminal yes The numbers 18 to 21 are for x86 and ARM computers; other processors use other numbers. Use the names in commands, kill -CONT, not kill -18: they work everywhere. man 7 signal has the full list.

Despite its name, kill sends a signal. Only SIGTERM, its default, asks the process to end. Command What it does kill -l Lists all the signals, with their numbers kill -l <NUMBER> Prints the name of a signal: kill -l 15 prints TERM kill <PID> Sends SIGTERM, the default, to the process kill -KILL <PID> Sends SIGKILL; kill -9 <PID> and kill -SIGKILL <PID> are the same kill -STOP <PID> Stops the process kill -CONT <PID> Continues the stopped process kill <PID1> <PID2> ... Sends the signal (SIGTERM, or the one you give) to several processes kill %<N> Sends the signal to job N of this shell (see jobs) Start sleep 1000 in the second terminal and send it signals from the first one: [student@fedora ~]$ pgrep sleep 3150 [student@fedora ~]$ kill -STOP 3150 [student@fedora ~]$ ps -o pid,stat,cmd -p 3150 PID STAT CMD 3150 T+ sleep 1000 [student@fedora ~]$ kill -CONT 3150 [student@fedora ~]$ ps -o pid,stat,cmd -p 3150 PID STAT CMD 3150 S+ sleep 1000 [student@fedora ~]$ kill 3150 [student@fedora ~]$ ps -o pid,stat,cmd -p 3150 PID STAT CMD SIGSTOP paused sleep: its state became T (stopped). SIGCONT continued it: it is waiting again (S). SIGTERM ended it: ps finds no process with this PID, and the second terminal prints Terminated. caution Use kill -KILL only when kill alone does not work. SIGTERM lets a program clean up before it ends (save its files, delete its temporary files), SIGKILL does not give it any chance.

The terminal turns some keys into signals for the process that runs in the foreground, the one that reads the keyboard: Keys Sends What happens, by default Ctrl+C SIGINT the foreground job ends Ctrl+\ SIGQUIT the foreground job ends, and the system saves a core dump Ctrl+Z SIGTSTP the foreground job is stopped, and the shell shows the prompt (see below) Ctrl+D no signal at the start of a line, end of file: the program reads nothing more [student@fedora ~]$ sleep 100 ^C [student@fedora ~]$ sleep 100 ^\Quit (core dumped) [student@fedora ~]$ sleep 100 ^Z [1]+ Stopped sleep 100 info Ctrl+D at the prompt of the shell is the end of its input: the shell ends, and the terminal window closes.

A program can replace the default action of a signal with its own signal handler: a part of its code that runs when the signal arrives, instead of the default action. A bash script sets a handler with trap, which runs a command or a function.. Create the file ~/lab04/stubborn.sh with nano: #!/bin/bash # the signal handler function no_interruptions_please () { echo "No interruptions please" } # register the signal handler trap no_interruptions_please SIGINT while true; do echo "working" sleep 1 done [student@fedora lab04]$ bash stubborn.sh working working ^CNo interruptions please working ^CNo interruptions please working ^\Quit (core dumped) The script writes working every second, forever. Ctrl+C sends SIGINT: the script runs its handler, prints the message, and keeps working. Ctrl+\ sends SIGQUIT, which has no handler: the script ends. Command What it does trap '<command>' <SIGNAL> Runs command when SIGNAL arrives; the quotes make it one word trap '' <SIGNAL> Ignores the signal trap - <SIGNAL> Goes back to the default action trap -p Prints the handlers info trap keeps the handler as text, and the shell runs that text when the signal arrives, as if you typed it then. The quotes decide when a variable in it is replaced: info SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be handled or ignored: trap cannot change them. This is why kill -KILL always ends a process.

A terminal has one job in the foreground: it reads the keyboard and receives the signals of the keys, and the shell waits for it to end before it shows the prompt again. All the commands you ran so far ran in the foreground. The shell can also start commands in the background. They are called jobs: the shell does not wait for them and shows the prompt right away, so they run at the same time as the commands you type. A job is either running or stopped. A command starts in the foreground (cmd) or in the background (cmd &). Ctrl+Z stops the foreground process and moves it to the background, bg continues a stopped job in the background, and fg brings a job back to the foreground. The rest of this section shows each of them.

Put & at the end of a command to run it in the background: [student@fedora ~]$ sleep 100 & [1] 4242 [student@fedora ~]$ sleep 200 & [2] 4250 [student@fedora ~]$ jobs [1]- Running sleep 100 & [2]+ Running sleep 200 & [student@fedora ~]$ echo $! 4250 [student@fedora ~]$ kill %1 [student@fedora ~]$ [1]- Terminated sleep 100 [1] is the job ID, which exists only in this shell; 4242 is the PID, for the whole system. jobs lists the jobs of this shell: + marks the current job (the last one), - the previous one. $! is the PID of the last job started with &. %1 means job 1: kill %1 sent SIGTERM to it, and the shell said that it ended when it showed the next prompt. Command What it does command & Runs command in the background, as a job jobs Lists the jobs of this shell jobs -l Lists them with their PIDs fg %<N> Brings job N to the foreground (and continues it, if it is stopped) bg %<N> Continues the stopped job N in the background kill %<N> Sends SIGTERM to job N fg, bg Without %<N>, they work on the current job, the one with + caution A job still writes to the same terminal: its output gets mixed with the commands you type. Redirect its output, for example find / -name passwd > found.txt 2> /dev/null &.

A command that runs in the foreground can be moved to the background later: press Ctrl+Z: the command is stopped (SIGTSTP), and the shell prints its job ID, for example [1]+ Stopped, and shows the prompt; find its job ID with jobs; run bg %<N>: the job continues (SIGCONT) in the background. tip fg %<N> brings it back to the foreground. [student@fedora ~]$ sleep 100 > /dev/null ^Z [1]+ Stopped sleep 100 > /dev/null [student@fedora ~]$ jobs [1]+ Stopped sleep 100 > /dev/null [student@fedora ~]$ bg %1 [1]+ sleep 100 > /dev/null & [student@fedora ~]$ jobs [1]+ Running sleep 100 > /dev/null & [student@fedora ~]$ fg %1 sleep 100 > /dev/null ^C After Ctrl+Z, sleep is stopped and the shell shows the prompt. bg continued it in the background (the shell prints it with an & at the end). fg brought it back to the foreground: the shell waits for it again, and Ctrl+C reaches it. tip Ctrl+Z is useful when you forgot the &, or when you want to leave a program for a moment, for example nano or less, run a command, then go back with fg.

documents.t: Only the foreground process can read the keyboard. A job that tries to read it receives SIGTTIN and is stopped: [student@fedora ~]$ cat & [1] 4321 [student@fedora ~]$ [1]+ Stopped cat [student@fedora ~]$ fg cat hello hello ^D cat without parameters reads the keyboard, so it stopped right away. fg brought it to the foreground, where it can read: it printed back every line, until Ctrl+D. info You cannot close a shell that still has stopped jobs at the first try: exit prints There are stopped jobs., and only a second exit closes it (and ends the jobs).

The kernel groups the processes of a terminal in two levels: Group What it is Its ID: the PID of its leader Its leader process group one job: all the processes of one command line, sleep 100 | cat is one group of two processes PGID: the first process of the command line the group leader session all the process groups of one terminal SID, the PID of the shell the session leader: the shell, s in STAT The terminal is the controlling terminal of the session. Its input, and the signals of the keys (Ctrl+C, Ctrl+Z, ...), go to the foreground process group, so they reach every process of the foreground job. + in the STAT column of ps marks the processes of the foreground group. [student@fedora ~]$ echo $$ 3000 [student@fedora ~]$ sleep 100 | cat & [1] 4243 [student@fedora ~]$ ps -o pid,ppid,pgid,sid,tty,stat,comm PID PPID PGID SID TT STAT COMMAND 3000 2990 3000 3000 pts/0 Ss bash 4242 3000 4242 3000 pts/0 S sleep 4243 3000 4242 3000 pts/0 S cat 4250 3000 4250 3000 pts/0 R+ ps bash is the session leader: its PID is the SID of all the processes of the terminal, and it has an s in STAT. sleep and cat are one job, so one group: 4242, the PID of sleep, the first process of the job. ps runs in the foreground (+), in a group of its own.

When the terminal closes, the kernel sends SIGHUP (hang up) to the session leader, the shell. The shell sends SIGHUP to all its jobs, and they end. A command started with nohup ignores SIGHUP, so it keeps running: [student@fedora ~]$ sleep 1000 & [1] 4300 [student@fedora ~]$ nohup sleep 2000 > /dev/null & [2] 4301 nohup: ignoring input Close this terminal window, and look for the two jobs from another terminal: [student@fedora ~]$ pgrep -a sleep 4301 sleep 2000 [student@fedora ~]$ ps -o pid,ppid,sid,tty,comm -p 4301 PID PPID SID TT COMMAND 4301 1 3000 ? sleep sleep 1000 received SIGHUP and ended. sleep 2000 ignored it and keeps running, without a terminal (?); its parent ended, so its new parent is PID 1. info If you do not redirect its output, nohup writes it into the file nohup.out, because the terminal will not exist anymore: nohup: ignoring input and appending output to 'nohup.out'. caution If the shell is killed with SIGKILL, it cannot send SIGHUP to its jobs anymore: they keep running, without a terminal, even without nohup.
