documents.t: Every process has an environment: a list of variables, each written as NAME=value. Programs read it to configure themselves: HOME tells them the home directory of the user, LANG the language, and PATH where to look for programs. The names are case-sensitive (HOME and home are different variables) and, by convention, in UPPER CASE. A process receives its environment from its parent when it starts: usually a copy of the parent's environment. From then on the two are separate: a change in one does not reach the other. Command What it does printenv Prints all the environment variables printenv <NAME> Prints the value of one variable env Prints all the environment variables, like printenv echo $NAME The shell replaces $NAME with its value, then echo prints it [student@fedora ~]$ printenv HOME /home/student [student@fedora ~]$ echo "I am $USER, my shell is $SHELL" I am student, my shell is /bin/bash [student@fedora ~]$ env | wc -l 35

The shell has two kinds of variables: shell variables: they exist only inside this shell; environment variables: they are part of the environment, so every command started from this shell receives a copy. Syntax What it does NAME=value Creates a shell variable, or changes the value of an existing variable export NAME Makes the variable an environment variable: every command started from now on receives it export NAME=value Both at once NAME=value command An environment variable only for command; the shell does not keep it unset NAME Deletes the variable, from the shell and from the environment $NAME Replaced by the shell with the value, or with nothing if the variable does not exist ${NAME} The same, with clear limits: "${NAME}_old" is the value followed by _old; "$NAME_old" is the variable NAME_old [student@fedora ~]$ GREETING=hello [student@fedora ~]$ echo $GREETING hello [student@fedora ~]$ bash -c 'echo "child: $GREETING"' child: [student@fedora ~]$ export GREETING [student@fedora ~]$ bash -c 'echo "child: $GREETING"' child: hello [student@fedora ~]$ unset GREETING [student@fedora ~]$ echo "[$GREETING]" [] GREETING=hello created a shell variable, and the shell replaced $GREETING with hello. bash -c '...' starts a new shell, a child, that runs the text between the quotes. The child did not receive GREETING: it was not part of the environment. After export, the child received a copy of it. After unset, the variable does not exist anymore, and $GREETING is replaced with nothing. danger No spaces around =. GREETING = hello runs the command GREETING, with the parameters = and hello: bash: GREETING: command not found. Put the value between quotes when it has spaces: GREETING="good morning". info A process can change only its own environment, and the environment of the children it starts after that. A child can never change a variable of its parent: this is why export and unset are commands of the shell, not programs.

NAME=value written before a command puts the variable only in the environment of that command: [student@fedora ~]$ date +%H:%M 11:47 [student@fedora ~]$ TZ=Asia/Tokyo date +%H:%M 18:47 [student@fedora ~]$ echo "[$TZ]" [] [student@fedora ~]$ ls /nope ls: cannot access '/nope': No such file or directory [student@fedora ~]$ LANG=ro_RO.UTF-8 ls /nope ls: nu se poate accesa '/nope': Fișier sau director inexistent TZ (time zone) changed the time zone only for that date; the shell did not keep it. LANG changed the language of the messages of ls (if the Romanian language is installed).

When the prompt shows up, the shell already has many variables, set when you logged in or by its startup files: Variable Value HOME your home directory, ~ USER your user name SHELL your shell, from /etc/passwd PWD, OLDPWD the current directory and the previous one (cd - goes to OLDPWD) PATH the directories with the programs, separated by : (see The PATH Search) LANG the language and the encoding of the characters PS1 the prompt; a shell variable, not exported tip PS1 is the text of the prompt, with some special sequences: \u is the user, \h the computer, \w the current directory, \$ is $ (or # for root). Try PS1='\u in \w \$ '. The change lasts until you close the terminal.

The shell sets a few more values that you can only read: Parameter Value $? the exit code of the last command: 0 means success, anything else an error $$ the PID of the shell $! the PID of the job most recently sent to the background, with & or bg [student@fedora ~]$ ls /nope ls: cannot access '/nope': No such file or directory [student@fedora ~]$ echo $? 2 [student@fedora ~]$ echo $? 0 ls failed, with the exit code 2. The second echo $? prints the exit code of the first echo, which succeeded: $? changes after every command.

Before a command starts, the shell reads the whole line and splits it into parts: [student@fedora lab04]$ LANG=C sort -r "$HOME/my notes.txt" my\ list.txt *.csv > sorted.txt 2> errors.txt Part In the example What it is assignments LANG=C NAME=value words at the start: variables only for this command the command sort the first word that is not an assignment or a redirect the parameters -r, "$HOME/my notes.txt", my\ list.txt, *.csv everything else: options, file names, texts redirects > sorted.txt, 2> errors.txt a redirect and the word after it; they are for the shell, not for the command, and can be anywhere Then, step by step: it splits the line into words at the spaces, except inside quotes and after a \; it sets apart the assignments and the redirects; it replaces $NAME and ~ with their values; it splits again the values of the variables that were not between quotes; it expands the globs (*.csv) into the names of the matching files; it removes the quotes and the \; it sets up the redirects and runs the command, with the words that are left as its parameters. sort receives 5 parameters: -r, /home/student/my notes.txt, my list.txt, a.csv and b.csv. It never sees the quotes, the $, the * or the redirects. tip To see the words that a command receives, use printf '[%s]\n' instead of the command: it prints every parameter between brackets, on its own line. [student@fedora lab04]$ printf '[%s]\n' -r "$HOME/my notes.txt" my\ list.txt *.csv [-r] [/home/student/my notes.txt] [my list.txt] [a.csv] [b.csv]

The redirects can be written anywhere in the line, even before the command, and the shell applies them from left to right: [student@fedora lab04]$ 2> errors.txt ls > list.txt /nope . [student@fedora lab04]$ ls /nope > all.txt 2>&1 [student@fedora lab04]$ ls /nope 2>&1 > all.txt ls: cannot access '/nope': No such file or directory The first line is the same as ls /nope . > list.txt 2> errors.txt. > all.txt 2>&1: first 1 goes to all.txt, then 2 goes where 1 goes now, also into all.txt. 2>&1 > all.txt: first 2 goes where 1 goes now, the display, then only 1 changes to all.txt. The error is on the display.

Some characters have a special meaning for the shell: the space, $, *, ?, [, {, ~, >, <, |, &, ;, #, ', " and \. Quotes and \ turn the special meaning off: Written as What it does '...' single quotes: everything inside is plain text, nothing is replaced "..." double quotes: $NAME is still replaced, but the result stays one word; globs are not expanded \ the next character is plain text: \ is a space that does not split, \$ is a $ With NAME="Alice Smith" (three spaces), this is what echo receives: You type echo receives Why echo $NAME Alice, Smith no quotes: replaced, then split at the spaces echo "$NAME" Alice Smith double quotes: replaced, one word, the spaces are kept echo '$NAME' $NAME single quotes: nothing is replaced echo \$NAME $NAME \$: the $ is just a character echo my\ file.txt my file.txt \ : the space does not split echo "\$NAME is $NAME" $NAME is Alice Smith inside "...", \$ is a $, $NAME is replaced echo "it's" 'say "hi"' it's, say "hi" each kind of quotes protects the other one echo 'a\b' a\b inside '...', \ is just a character [student@fedora ~]$ NAME="Alice Smith" [student@fedora ~]$ echo $NAME Alice Smith [student@fedora ~]$ echo "$NAME" Alice Smith [student@fedora ~]$ printf '[%s]\n' $NAME [Alice] [Smith] echo $NAME received two words and printed them with one space between them: the three spaces were lost. tip Put every variable between double quotes, "$NAME", unless you really want it split into words. A file name with a space in a variable breaks a command without them: rm $FILE with FILE="my notes.txt" tries to delete my and notes.txt.

A glob is a pattern for file names. The shell replaces it with the names of the matching files, in alphabetical order, before the command starts. In this directory: [student@fedora glob]$ ls docs notes.txt photo1.png photo2.png photo3.png photoA.png report.md todo.txt Glob Matches echo receives *.txt *: any characters, or none (but not /) notes.txt, todo.txt photo?.png ?: exactly one character photo1.png, photo2.png, photo3.png, photoA.png photo[12].png [12]: one character, 1 or 2 photo1.png, photo2.png photo[0-9].png [0-9]: one character in the range photo1.png, photo2.png, photo3.png photo[!0-9].png [!0-9]: one character not in the range ([^0-9] also works) photoA.png docs/**/*.txt **: any directories, at any depth (needs shopt -s globstar) docs/2026/exam.txt, docs/plan.txt {a,b,c}.pdf {...}: one word for each, even if the file does not exist a.pdf, b.pdf, c.pdf *.pdf no file matches *.pdf, the glob as it is caution When no file matches, bash gives the glob as it is to the command: ls *.pdf prints ls: cannot access '*.pdf': No such file or directory. Other shells, like zsh, print an error and do not run the command at all. info * and ? do not match the . at the beginning of a hidden file: * does not include .bashrc, but .* does. {...} is not a glob: it makes the words even if there are no files, which is useful to create them, for example mkdir -p 2026/{jan,feb,mar} or touch photo{4..6}.png ({4..6} is 4 5 6). ** works only after shopt -s globstar; without it, it is the same as *. Between quotes, a glob is plain text: echo "*.txt" prints *.txt. This is how you give a pattern to a command that understands it by itself, like find . -name "*.txt".

Not every command is a program: Kind What it is Examples Help built-in command part of the shell: it runs inside it, without a new process cd, export, unset, exit, jobs, fg, bg, trap, type help <name> some are built in only to be faster, and also exist as programs echo, printf, kill, pwd external command an executable file on the disk, found in PATH; the shell starts it as a child process ls, sort, grep, sleep, bash man <name> type tells which one a command is: [student@fedora ~]$ type cd cd is a shell builtin [student@fedora ~]$ type sort sort is /usr/bin/sort [student@fedora ~]$ type ls ls is aliased to `ls --color=auto' [student@fedora ~]$ type -a echo echo is a shell builtin echo is /usr/bin/echo cd is built in, sort is the file /usr/bin/sort. ls is an alias: a short name for another command line, here ls --color=auto. -a shows all the meanings of the name: echo is built in, and there is also a program with the same name. The shell uses the first one. info cd, export, unset and exit must be built in: they change the shell itself, its current directory, its variables, or stop it. A program started by the shell is a child process, and a child cannot change its parent.

The kernel can only start a program from its path. When the first word is a name, the shell has to find the file: if the word has a /, it is a path: absolute (/usr/bin/sort) or relative to the current directory (./hello, bin/hello, ../tools/hello), used as it is; otherwise, if it is an alias or a built-in command, the shell runs it itself; otherwise, the shell searches the directories of the PATH variable, from left to right, and runs the first file with that name; if no directory has it: command not found. [student@fedora ~]$ echo $PATH /home/student/.local/bin:/home/student/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin [student@fedora ~]$ cd ~/lab04 [student@fedora lab04]$ ls bin hello [student@fedora lab04]$ hello bash: hello: command not found [student@fedora lab04]$ bin/hello Hello! [student@fedora lab04]$ PATH="$PATH:$HOME/lab04/bin" [student@fedora lab04]$ hello Hello! [student@fedora lab04]$ type hello hello is /home/student/lab04/bin/hello The shell does not look in the current directory, so hello alone was not found. bin/hello has a /, so it is a path, and the shell ran it. After adding ~/lab04/bin at the end of PATH, the shell found hello there. caution Add directories to PATH, never replace it: PATH=~/lab04/bin alone leaves the shell without /usr/bin, and ls, cat and almost every other command become command not found. Close the terminal and open a new one to get the old PATH back. tip On Fedora, ~/.local/bin and ~/bin are already in PATH: copy a program of your own there and it works from any directory, in every new terminal.

Problem Solution Ctrl+C does not stop a program It handles or ignores SIGINT: try Ctrl+\, or Ctrl+Z followed by kill %1; as a last resort, kill -KILL <PID> from another terminal kill does not end a process It handles SIGTERM: use kill -KILL <PID> A stopped process does not react to kill It receives the signal when it continues: kill -CONT <PID>, or use kill -KILL <PID> bash: kill: (4242) - Operation not permitted The process belongs to another user bash: kill: %1: no such job or fg: current: no such job The job belongs to another terminal (every shell has its own jobs), or it has already ended; use the PID [1]+ Stopped right after command & The job tries to read the keyboard: bring it to the foreground with fg, or redirect its input There are stopped jobs. when you close the shell Continue or end them (fg, kill %N); a second exit ends them A job writes over the commands you type Redirect its output to a file, or to /dev/null bash: NAME: command not found after NAME = value No spaces around = A child does not see a variable It is a shell variable: export it bash: <command>: command not found Check the name, then echo $PATH: the directory of the program is not in PATH, or PATH was replaced; open a new terminal A file in the current directory is command not found The shell does not search the current directory: run it as ./name cannot access '*.pdf' No file matches the glob, so the command received it as it is A name with a space becomes two files Put it, or the variable that holds it, between double quotes The shell shows > and waits A quote is not closed: close it, or press Ctrl+C and type the line again

The exercises get harder as you go: 🧪 First Steps (exercises 1 - 23) goes once through everything in this lab, with easy exercises; 🏠 Going Further (exercises 24 - 51) has more exercises to do at home, harder as you go; 📝 Challenges (exercises 52 - 62) has the hardest ones. Exercise 1 creates the files and directories that all the other exercises start from. Run the commands in ~/lab04, unless the exercise says otherwise. If you change or delete one of the files from exercise 1, run its commands again to get it back. Some exercises ask for things that the lab does not show you, for example an option that is not in the tables above. Find it in the manual page of the command (man <command>), as explained in Searching in a Manual Page in lab 02. jobs, fg, bg, trap, export and the other built-in commands do not have a manual page of their own: use help <command>, for example help trap, or search man bash. Keep two terminals side by side in Sway: the first one to run the commands, and the second one to run the commands that you inspect, or to check the results. Many exercises use the PID of a process: it is different on your computer, use the one that pgrep, ps or $! prints for you. danger Do not use sudo to send signals: sudo kill can end the processes of the system. Send signals only to your own processes, and check the PID twice before kill -KILL.

The practice tree: run these commands to create the files used in the exercises (copy them from the browser with Ctrl+C and paste them in the terminal with Ctrl+Shift+V): mkdir -p ~/lab04/bin ~/lab04/glob/docs/2026 cd ~/lab04 printf 'pear
fig
' > 'my notes.txt' printf 'cherry
Banana
apple
' > 'my list.txt' printf 'banana,3
apple,5
' > a.csv printf 'cherry,1
kiwi,7
' > b.csv printf '#!/bin/bash
echo Hello!
' > bin/hello chmod +x bin/hello cat > stubborn.sh << 'EOF' #!/bin/bash # the signal handler function no_interruptions_please () { echo "No interruptions please" } # register the signal handler trap no_interruptions_please SIGINT while true; do echo "working" sleep 1 done EOF cd ~/lab04/glob touch notes.txt todo.txt report.md photo1.png photo2.png photo3.png photoA.png docs/plan.txt docs/2026/exam.txt cd ~/lab04 run tree in ~/lab04; print stubborn.sh with cat. Check: you see bin/hello, the two .csv files, my list.txt, my notes.txt, stubborn.sh and the glob directory with 9 files; stubborn.sh is the script from Handling a Signal. chmod +x makes hello a program that can be run (you will learn about it in the lab about permissions). → Navigation Terminals Which terminal: print the terminal of the shell, in both terminals; list the pseudo terminals in /dev/pts; open a third terminal and list them again, then close it. Check: each shell has its own /dev/pts/<n>; the third terminal adds one more number to the list, and its number disappears after you close it. → Terminal Emulators Write to another terminal: find the terminal of the second shell, with tty; from the first terminal, write hello from the first terminal into the second one, with echo and a redirect. Check: the text appears in the second terminal, without anything typed there. → Terminal Emulators A virtual terminal: in a terminal in Sway, find out in which virtual terminal Sway runs, with loginctl; switch to the third virtual terminal with Ctrl+Alt+F3 (Host+F3 in VirtualBox); log in as student, print the name of the terminal and list its processes with ps; log out with exit; switch back to Sway, using the number that loginctl printed. Check: VTNr is 1 or 2; tty prints /dev/tty3, and ps shows a bash on tty3; after exit, the terminal asks for a login again; back in Sway, your windows are exactly as you left them. → Virtual Terminals Signals The list of signals: list all the signals with kill; print the name of signal 9 and the number of SIGCONT, with kill -l. Check: signal 9 is KILL, and CONT is 18. → Sending a Signal Stop and continue: in the second terminal, run sleep 1000; in the first terminal, find its PID and stop it with a signal; show its state with ps -o pid,stat,cmd -p <PID>, and look at the second terminal; continue it, show its state again, and run jobs in the second terminal; end it with kill %1 in the second terminal. Check: the state is T after SIGSTOP and S after SIGCONT, without the +. As soon as sleep stopped, the second shell printed [1]+ Stopped (signal), took the terminal back and showed the prompt, so after SIGCONT, jobs shows sleep as Running in the background. → Sending a Signal Keys and signals: run sleep 100 and end it with Ctrl+C; run it again and end it with Ctrl+\; run it again and stop it with Ctrl+Z; list the jobs. Check: the terminal shows ^C after Ctrl+C, Quit (core dumped) after Ctrl+\ (only Quit if core dumps are turned off), and Stopped after Ctrl+Z; sleep is still in the list of jobs. End it with kill %1. → Keys That Send Signals A stubborn script: run bash stubborn.sh; press Ctrl+C a few times; stop it with Ctrl+\. Check: Ctrl+C prints No interruptions please and the script keeps working; Ctrl+\ ends it. → Handling a Signal Foreground and background Two jobs: start sleep 300 and sleep 400 in the background; list the jobs, and then the jobs with their PIDs; print the PID of the last job with $!; end the first job using its job ID; end the second job too, and list the jobs again. Check: jobs shows [1] and [2], with + at [2]; $! is the PID of sleep 400; after the next command, the shell prints [1]- Terminated; at the end, jobs prints nothing. → Starting a Job To the background and back: run sleep 200 > /dev/null in the foreground; stop it with the keyboard; continue it in the background, and check with jobs that it runs; bring it back to the foreground, and end it with the keyboard. Check: jobs shows Stopped, then Running; after fg, the prompt does not show up until you press Ctrl+C. → Stopping and Continuing The current job: start sleep 300, sleep 400 and sleep 500 in the background; list the jobs, and find the current one; run fg without a job ID, and end the job with Ctrl+C; list the jobs again, and end the others with kill. Check: the current job (+) is sleep 500, the last one started, and fg brought it to the foreground; after it ended, sleep 400 became the current job. → Starting a Job Sessions Session and groups: print the PID of your shell; start sleep 100 | cat in the background; list the processes of the terminal with the columns pid, ppid, pgid, sid, tty, stat and comm. Check: all the processes have the PID of the shell as their SID; sleep and cat have the same PGID, the PID of sleep; bash has s and ps has + in STAT. → Sessions and Process Groups Close the terminal: open a new terminal and start sleep 1000 & and nohup sleep 2000 > /dev/null & in it; close the window of this terminal; in another terminal, look for the two sleep processes; end sleep 2000 with kill. Check: only sleep 2000 is still running, without a terminal (?). Its parent ended, so it was adopted: its new parent is PID 1, or a process that adopts orphans, like systemd --user (see which one with ps -o pid,comm -p <PPID>). → Closing the Terminal Variables Read variables: print HOME, USER and SHELL with printenv; print the sentence I am student and I live in /home/student with echo and the variables USER and HOME; count the environment variables. Check: the sentence has your user and your home directory; there are a few dozen variables. → Environment Variables Shell variable or environment variable: set the shell variable COLOR to blue, and print it; check with printenv COLOR and with bash -c 'echo "$COLOR"' whether it is in the environment; export it, and check again; delete it, and print it again. Check: before export, printenv prints nothing and the child prints an empty line; after it, both print blue; after unset, echo prints an empty line. → Shell Variables and export Only for one command: print the time with date +%H:%M; print the time in Tokyo and in New York (America/New_York), by setting TZ only for date; print TZ. Check: the three times are different, and TZ is empty in the shell. → A Variable for One Command Exit codes: run ls ~/lab04 and print its exit code; run ls /nope and print its exit code; run grep apple a.csv and grep pear a.csv, and print the exit code after each of them; run echo $? twice in a row. Check: ls has the exit code 0, then 2; grep has 0 when it finds the text and 1 when it does not; the second echo $? always prints 0. → Special Parameters The command line The words of a command: Use printf '[%s]
' to see the words that the shell gives to a command: printf '[%s]
' one two three; printf '[%s]
' "one two three"; printf '[%s]
' ~ "~" '$HOME' "$HOME". Check: the first line gives 3 words, the second one only 1, with the spaces kept; ~ and "$HOME" become /home/student, "~" and '$HOME' stay as they are. → The Command Line · Quoting and Escaping Quotes and variables: set NAME="Alice Smith"; print it with echo, without quotes, between double quotes and between single quotes; print the text $NAME is Alice Smith with a single echo and one pair of double quotes. Check: without quotes, the three spaces become one; between double quotes they are kept; between single quotes echo prints $NAME; the last echo prints $NAME is Alice Smith, with the three spaces. → Quoting and Escaping A dollar sign: Print the text The price is $5 with echo: first with double quotes and nothing else, and see what goes wrong; with single quotes; with a \ and no quotes; with double quotes and a \. Check: step 1 prints The price is: the shell replaced $5 with nothing. $5 is the fifth positional parameter, a parameter given to a script, and it is empty in your shell. Single quotes and \ turn off the meaning of $, so steps 2, 3 and 4 print The price is $5. → Quoting and Escaping Globs: Go to ~/lab04/glob and, with echo, print: all the .png files; the photos with a single digit after photo; the photos whose name does not have a digit after photo; all the files whose name has exactly 8 characters (count the extension too); all the .pdf files; the names photo7.png and photo8.png, with {...}. Check: photoA.png is in the first and the third list, not in the second one; the fourth list is todo.txt; the fifth echo prints *.pdf, because no file matches; the last one prints both names, even if the files do not exist. → Globbing Built-in or external: find out with type what cd, ls, sort, type and sleep are; show all the meanings of kill and of echo; print the PATH, and find in which of its directories sort is. Check: cd and type are built in, ls is an alias, sort and sleep are in /usr/bin; kill and echo are built in, and also exist as programs in /usr/bin. For a program you already ran, type says hashed, for example sleep is hashed (/usr/bin/sleep): the shell remembers where it found it. → Built-in and External Commands · The PATH Search Command not found: run sl (a typo of ls), and print the exit code; find out with type whether sl exists; run /usr/bin/nope, and print the exit code. Check: the shell searched all the directories of PATH and found no sl: the exit code is 127, the code of the shell for command not found; /usr/bin/nope is a path that does not exist, and its exit code is 127 too. If the shell offers to install a package for sl, answer N. → The PATH Search · Special Parameters

The terminal in ps: list the processes of the terminal with ps; print the 0, 1 and 2 file descriptors of the shell, from /proc/$$/fd. Check: the TTY column of ps and the three links in /proc/$$/fd show the same pseudo terminal as tty. → Terminal Emulators · The /proc File System Names and numbers: in the second terminal, run sleep 1000; in the first terminal, end it with kill, giving the signal SIGTERM by its number; run sleep 1000 again and end it, giving SIGTERM by its name, with the SIG in front. Check: both times the second terminal prints Terminated: kill -15, kill -TERM and kill -SIGTERM send the same signal. → Sending a Signal End a process: in the second terminal, run sleep 1000; in the first terminal, end it with kill and its default signal; run sleep 1000 again, and end it with SIGKILL. Check: the second terminal prints Terminated the first time and Killed the second time. → Sending a Signal SIGINT from kill: in the second terminal, run bash stubborn.sh; in the first terminal, find the PID of the script (look for stubborn with pgrep -f); send it SIGINT with kill; end it with SIGTERM. Check: SIGINT sent with kill has the same effect as Ctrl+C: the message appears in the second terminal; SIGTERM ends the script, because it has no handler for it. → Sending a Signal · Handling a Signal Leave an editor for a moment: open stubborn.sh with nano; stop nano with Ctrl+Z (if it does not stop, press Ctrl+T, then Ctrl+Z), and run ls; go back to nano, and quit it; do the same with less stubborn.sh. Check: nano and less come back exactly as you left them. → Stopping and Continuing A job that reads: start cat in the background; list the jobs; bring it to the foreground, type two lines, and end its input. Check: cat is Stopped right away; in the foreground it prints back every line you type, and Ctrl+D ends it. → Jobs That Read the Keyboard A job with its own output: search the whole file system for files named passwd with find, in the background, with the output in found.txt and the errors thrown away; run jobs until the job is Done; print found.txt. Check: nothing from find appears in the terminal, and found.txt has /etc/passwd. → Starting a Job · Special Files Jobs belong to a shell: in the second terminal, start sleep 600 in the background; in the first terminal, list the jobs; in the first terminal, find the PID of sleep 600 with pgrep -f 'sleep 600', and end it. Check: jobs prints nothing in the first terminal: every shell has only its own jobs. kill %1 does not work there, but kill <PID> does, and the second terminal prints Terminated after its next command. → Starting a Job One key, the whole group: run sleep 100 | sleep 200 in the second terminal; in the first terminal, list the two processes with pgrep -a sleep; press Ctrl+C in the second terminal, and list them again. Check: both sleep processes ended at the same time: the signal reached the whole foreground group. → Sessions and Process Groups Spaces around =: run GREETING = hello; run GREETING=good morning; set GREETING to good morning correctly, and print it. Check: the first command is command not found for GREETING, the second one for morning, because the shell ran morning with GREETING=good in its environment. → Shell Variables and export The previous directory: go to /etc, then to ~/lab04; print PWD and OLDPWD; run cd -, and print them again. Check: cd - takes you back to /etc, and the two variables swap their values. → Variables Defined by the System Inherited by the children: export the variable LEVEL with the value 1; start a new bash (just type bash), print LEVEL, and set it to 2; leave the child with exit, and print LEVEL again. Check: the child printed 1, received from its parent; after exit, the parent still has 1: the child changed only its own copy. → Shell Variables and export The PID of the shell: print the PID of your shell with $$, and compare it with the line of bash printed by ps; start a new bash (type bash), and print $$ and ps again; leave it with exit, and print $$ once more. Check: inside the new bash, $$ is a different number, and ps shows two bash processes; after exit, $$ is the first number again. → Special Parameters The environment from /proc: in the second terminal, run MESSAGE=secret sleep 1000; in the first terminal, find the PID of sleep and show its environment from /proc/<PID>/environ, with the \0 bytes replaced by new lines (look in man tr for how to replace a character), keeping only the line of MESSAGE; look for MESSAGE in the environment of the second shell in the same way. Check: sleep has MESSAGE=secret, the shell of the second terminal does not. /proc/<PID>/environ shows the environment that a process received when it started: a variable that the shell exports later does not appear there. → A Variable for One Command · The /proc File System The language of the messages: run ls /nope with LANG set to ro_RO.UTF-8 only for ls; sort my list.txt with sort (the name has a space), then with LANG=C only for sort. Check: the prompt changes right away and shows ~/lab04/glob; printenv PS1 prints nothing: it is a shell variable. Close the terminal to get the old prompt back. → Variables Defined by the System Split a command line: Without running it, write the words that sort receives, and where its output and its errors go, for: LANG=C sort -r "$HOME/my notes.txt" my\ list.txt *.csv > sorted.txt 2> errors.txt then replace sort with printf '[%s]\n' and remove the > sorted.txt redirect, to check your answer. Check: 5 words: -r, /home/student/my notes.txt, my list.txt, a.csv and b.csv. The output of sort goes into sorted.txt and its errors into errors.txt; LANG=C is only in its environment. → The Command Line Redirects anywhere: run 2> errors.txt ls > list.txt /nope .; print the two files; write the same command with the redirects at the end. Check: list.txt has the files of ~/lab04 and errors.txt the error for /nope, both times. → The Order of Redirects The order of redirects: run ls /nope . > all.txt 2>&1 and print all.txt; run ls /nope . 2>&1 > all.txt and print all.txt. Check: the first time, both the list and the error are in the file; the second time, the error is on the display, because 2 was copied from 1 before 1 changed. → The Order of Redirects Variables with spaces: set FILE="my notes.txt"; run cat $FILE, then cat "$FILE"; set OPTS="-t, -k2 -n" and sort a.csv and b.csv with sort $OPTS, then with sort "$OPTS". Check: cat $FILE looks for my and notes.txt; cat "$FILE" works. sort $OPTS receives three options and sorts the lines by the number after the comma: cherry,1, banana,3, apple,5, kiwi,7. sort "$OPTS" receives one word, so -t takes , -k2 -n as the separator: sort: multi-character tab. → Quoting and Escaping Special names: create the files rock & roll.txt, it's mine.txt and $HOME.txt with one touch command; list them with ls, then with ls -N; delete them with one rm command, this time using \ instead of quotes. Check: ls shows the names between quotes, only for display; ls -N shows exactly these three names, and $HOME.txt is not /home/student.txt. rm deletes all three. → Quoting and Escaping Names from braces: in ~/lab04, create the directories trips/2025 and trips/2026 with one mkdir -p command and {...}; create the files jan.txt, feb.txt and mar.txt in both directories, with one touch command; show the result with tree trips. Check: the first list has docs/2026/exam.txt, docs/plan.txt, notes.txt and todo.txt; photo?.png now matches 7 files; ~/.* has .bashrc and the other hidden files, but not . and ..: the option globskipdots is on by default since bash 5.2. → Globbing Glob or text: In ~/lab04/glob: run find . -name *.txt; run find . -name "*.txt"; find out why the first one fails, using printf '[%s]\n' instead of find. Check: hello alone is command not found, but bin/hello, /home/student/lab04/bin/hello and, in bin, ./hello work; after the change of PATH, hello works from any directory, and type hello shows its path (hello is hashed (...), because you already ran it). → The PATH Search A broken PATH: Open a new terminal: set PATH to /tmp, and run ls; run /usr/bin/ls; run cd ~ and echo $HOME; close the terminal. Check: ls is command not found, but /usr/bin/ls works, because it is a path; cd and echo still work, because they are built in. → The PATH Search Your own bin: create ~/.local/bin, if it does not exist, and copy bin/hello there; open a new terminal and run hello from your home directory; find out from where it was started. Check: type hello prints hello is hashed (/home/student/.local/bin/hello): on Fedora, this directory is already in PATH. → The PATH Search Who wins: create the directory ~/lab04/first with two programs, ls and echo, that print Not the real ls! and Not the real echo! (do as for bin/hello in exercise 1: printf with single quotes, then chmod +x); add ~/lab04/first at the beginning of PATH; run ls, \ls, /usr/bin/ls and echo hi; run type -a ls and type -a echo; close the terminal. Check: ls and \ls (which skips the alias) both print Not the real ls!: the alias only replaces the word ls with ls --color=auto, and this ls is still searched in PATH, where ~/lab04/first comes first. /usr/bin/ls is a path, so there is no search. echo hi prints hi: a built-in command comes before the PATH search. type -a lists the meanings in the order the shell tries them. → The PATH Search

Ignore and restore: edit stubborn.sh so that it also ignores SIGTERM; run it in the second terminal, and try to end it from the first terminal with kill, then with kill -KILL; in your shell, make SIGINT print Not now, press Ctrl+C at the prompt, then go back to the default action. Check: the window closed, but both sleep processes are still running, without a terminal; their new parent is PID 1, or a process that adopts orphans, like systemd --user. The shell could not send SIGHUP to them. → Closing the Terminal A session in text mode: log in on /dev/tty3 (Ctrl+Alt+F3) and start sleep 1000 &; go back to Sway, and list the processes of that terminal with ps -t tty3 -o pid,ppid,sid,stat,comm; find the session leader of tty3, and its parent; go back to tty3, end sleep, and log out. Check: bash is the session leader: it has s in STAT, and its PID is the SID of sleep; its parent is login, which checked your password and started it. → Virtual Terminals · Sessions and Process Groups Why cd is built in: Fedora also has a program called cd, in /usr/bin. find it with type -a cd; go to your home directory, run /usr/bin/cd /tmp, and print the current directory; explain what happened. Check: in the old terminal, lt is command not found at first: bash reads ~/.bashrc only when it starts, or when you ask it to with source; in the new terminal, and after source, lt lists the files, the newest first, and type prints lt is aliased to `ls -lt'. → Built-in and External Commands An empty environment: Look in man env for the option that starts a command with an empty environment. run env with this option, followed by bash -c 'echo "[$HOME] [$PATH]"'; run env with this option, followed by bash -c 'ls'; run env with this option, followed by TZ=Asia/Tokyo /usr/bin/date. Check: HOME is empty, PATH has a default value that bash sets by itself, so ls still works; date prints the time in Tokyo: the only variable it received is TZ. → Environment Variables Background PIDs: start sleep 300 | sleep 400 in the background; print $!, and list the jobs with their PIDs; end the whole job with one kill, using the job ID. Check: $! is the PID of sleep 400, the last process of the pipe; jobs -l shows both PIDs; kill %1 ends both processes, because it sends the signal to the whole process group. → Starting a Job · Sessions and Process Groups Count with globs: Go to /usr/bin and, without ls or find, using only a glob: print, one per line, the programs whose name starts with g and has exactly 4 characters (use printf '%s\n'); count them, in the same command line; do the same for the programs whose name ends with a digit; go back to ~/lab04.
